rows.assumption: A-1 — Slow deploys cost the business a material amount
A-3 — Every deploy has to run the full test suite
A-4 — Every deploy needs a coordinated restart of the application
A-5 — The 45-minute pipeline is what holds the cadence at 2 deploys a day
A-6 — The pipeline splits into about 5 min setup, 35 min tests and 5 min deploy/restart
A-7 — Each engineer produces about 1 deployable change per working day
A-8 — Each engineer waits on CI about 2 times a day and half of that waiting is lost
A-9 — The split extracts about 60% of the 350 KLOC at roughly 2 KLOC per engineer-week (range 1–5)
A-10 — Deploys and CI waits happen only inside an 8-hour (480-minute) working day
A-11 — Each service's test time is proportional to its share of the code
A-12 — A deploy pipeline should run at no more than 50% utilisation so a queue does not form
A-13 — The test suite can run on parallel workers with no dependence on test order or shared state
A-14 — Production deploys run one pipeline at a time
A-15 — Most changes stay inside one of the four domains
A-16 — With 8 shards, each run uses 8 × 5 + 35 + 5 = 80 runner-minutes of CI compute, against 45 today
A-17 — Changes become ready at times spread evenly across the day
A-18 — Time lost waiting scales in proportion to pipeline duration
A-19 — A checkout touches catalog, cart and fulfillment code

chains.title: The 45-minute pipeline does not cap deploys at 2 a day
Most of a change's lead time is spent waiting for the next deploy, not in the pipeline
The 45 minutes becomes the binding limit only when each change deploys on its own
Splitting the tests by service saves no more time than splitting them by shard
The cost of the 45-minute wait could be anywhere from minor to large, because nobody has measured it
Microservices are a large investment with a slow payback
Speeding up the pipeline inside the monolith pays back in weeks, at least 6 times faster than microservices
Microservices swap restart coordination for version coordination and add new failure modes to the revenue path
Recommend option B — speed up the pipeline and raise deploy cadence inside the monolith
Waiting for the next batch outweighs pipeline time whenever deploys are spaced more than twice the pipeline time apart
Any test-time gain from a service split is also available to the monolith as shards
Splitting the app adds runtime failure modes to every call path the split crosses

conclusion.recommended: Keep the monolith and go after lead time where it is actually spent. Run the suite in parallel on 8 shards (target ≤20 min, about 14.375 min), add changed-file test selection, and replace the coordinated restart with a rolling restart. Then move toward deploying each change on its own, enforcing a 20-minute pipeline budget in CI (chain C9).

dead_ends: Microservices as the fix for deploy speed
Flaky reruns as a hidden capacity cap
Merges cluster before deploys, so the pipeline dominates lead time
Merge-queue batching instead of a faster pipeline
Smaller per-service restarts as the decisive microservice advantage
